title: Email change

import { Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import routesTs from '../../../../snippets/build/email-change/routes.ts?raw';

The core has four flows for changing the account's email: `requestEmailChange`, `confirmEmailChangeCode` (or `confirmEmailChangeLink`), and `revertEmailChange`. Why each rule is there is in [Email change](/auth/learn/email-change/). This guide builds on [A Node server with Redis and Prisma](/auth/build/node-server/).

## What it needs

- **A user store with `changeEmail`.** `PrismaUserStore` and `MemoryUserStore` have it. The method is optional on the `UserStore` port so older adapters still compile, and the email change flows throw an `AuthConfigError` without it. A store of your own must keep the email column unique and pass the `changeEmail` cases of `userStoreConformance` (see [Writing a store adapter](/auth/build/store-adapter/)).
- **`urls.revertEmailChange`.** The link mailed to the old address. The flows throw an `AuthConfigError` without it. Put the token in the fragment, as the node-server sample does, and send `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`.
- **Templates** for four mail events: `email-change-confirm`, `email-change-in-use`, `email-changed` and `email-change-reverted` ([Mail](/auth/build/mail/)).

No new table: the code, the revert link, the hold on the old address, the block after a revert and the lockout after a refused revert are rows of the one-time token table you already have, under their own purposes. Every row is filed under a real user id, so the `user` relation that `auth.prisma` suggests for cascading deletes works; the hold is found by the SHA-256 of its address in the hash column.

## Every path that creates users

The library holds the old address for its owner while the revert link lives, and its own sign-up and email change flows refuse a held address as taken. Paths your app owns do not go through those flows: invitations, an admin "create user", a first sign-in through SSO, imports. Each must call `auth.isAddressHeld(email)` and refuse a held address the way it refuses a taken one, before it creates the user or gives an account that address. If one of them does not, the old address can get an account, and the owner's revert cannot finish (below).

## The routes

<Code code={routesTs} lang="ts" title="src/routes/email.ts" />

**Request.** The session must be live and its last credential proof, read from the stored session, younger than `session.freshAuthAge` (10 minutes by default), or the answer is `fresh_auth_required`: send the user through `auth.reauthenticate` and retry. With the [two-factor plugin](/auth/build/two-factor/) on and a factor confirmed, the request also needs a step-up held by the session or a code in `secondFactor`, or it answers `second_factor_required`. A new address that already has an account gets the same success answer and the same `expiresAt` as a free one, and its owner gets `email-change-in-use` instead of a code, so show "check the new address" either way. A new request replaces a pending one; a password change or reset, or signing out of other devices or everywhere, voids it. While the revert link of an earlier change is live, a new request answers `forbidden` (reason `email_change_pending_revert` in the audit row): tell the user they can change the address again once the link sent to their old address expires. Requests are limited per account (3 an hour) and per new address (3 an hour, from every account).

**Confirm.** The code is typed in a live signed-in session of the same account; in link mode (`emailChange.kind: 'link'`, with `urls.confirmEmailChange`) the link works only in such a session too, and is left unspent anywhere else, a revoked session included. On success the account moves to the new address, which is marked verified; every session of the account is revoked and the caller's is re-issued, so set the cookie of the session it returns. Reset and verification tokens mailed to the old address die, and the old address gets `email-changed` at once. If another account took the new address after the request, the answer is `email_in_use`; the confirmer has just proved that mailbox, so the answer tells them nothing about anyone else.

**Revert.** The old address's mail carries a link valid for 7 days (`emailChange.revertTtl`, which cannot be shorter). It needs no session. It moves the account back to the old address and removes the password in one write, then revokes every session, voids every reset, verification and pending change token. Second factors stay: a revert cannot tell the owner's factor from one an intruder enrolled, and whoever reads the old mailbox must not be able to strip the owner's (A063). The next sign-in therefore fails until the user resets the password, and the reset goes to the restored address: tell them so on the page. The address the account lost is blocked for this account for 30 days (`emailChange.blockAfterRevert`), and the audit row `email.change_reverted` carries `review: true`. Route it to whoever looks at suspicious accounts.

If the old address has an account again (an app path that skipped `isAddressHeld`, a race with sign-up, or a direct store write), the revert answers `email_in_use` with reason `email_revert_address_taken`. It has still removed the password and revoked every session and pending token, and the `email.change_revert_failed` row carries `review: true` and `lockedOut: true`. Tell the user to contact support.

**The lockout after a refused revert.** The account still names the intruder's address, so the revert also locks it out. The lockout never lapses on its own. While it lives, no session is issued for the account by any flow or plugin (your own SSO through `issueSession` included; a login answers like a wrong password), a reset request for it sends nothing (the request answers as always), and a reset link for it answers `invalid_token` (refused before the new password is hashed, so it costs what a dead link costs). The owner's revert link lives as long as the lockout. Both are stored to expire at the start of 9999-12-31 UTC rather than renewed, because a renewal would depend on something running in time; every SQL date column (MySQL's `DATETIME` included) and a Redis TTL can hold that value, and the token store conformance suite checks it. If your own token store sweeps rows by `expiresAt`, it keeps these. It ends in one of two ways:

- the owner clicks the same link again once the old address is free, which restores it and ends the lockout;
- support calls `auth.clearEmailRevertLockout({ userId, meta })`, which writes `email.revert_lockout_cleared` with `review: true`. Do this only once the account is on an address its owner controls: clearing it while the account still names the intruder's address hands that address a working reset.

For support: find the account from the `email.change_revert_failed` row, free the old address (it belongs to whoever created the account on it), and send the owner back to their link. If the old address cannot be freed, move the account to an address the owner controls in your store, then clear the lockout and have the owner reset the password.

**What is not atomic.** Each flow is a series of store calls, not a transaction. Confirm writes the revert link and the hold before it moves the address, and revokes sessions after; a store error between leaves at worst an unmailed revert link for an address that did not move, which blocks nothing. Revert removes the password in the same write as the restore, sets the lockout if the restore was refused, and revokes sessions right after; a store error after the restore leaves the link unspent, and clicking it again runs every step again.

## Answers

| Code | From | Show |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fresh_auth_required` | request | the password prompt, then retry |
| `second_factor_required`, `invalid_second_factor` | request | the code prompt, then retry |
| `invalid_email` | request | "enter a valid address" (also for the account's current address) |
| `forbidden` | request | an earlier change can still be reverted, the address was blocked after a revert, or one of your hooks refused |
| `invalid_token` | confirm, revert | "the code or link is wrong or expired" |
| `email_in_use` | confirm, revert | the address was taken meanwhile |
| `session_expired` | any | sign in again |
| `rate_limited` | any | "try again later", with `retryAfterSeconds` |

## Options

| Option | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `emailChange.kind` | `'code'` | `'link'` needs `urls.confirmEmailChange`. |
| `emailChange.ttl` | `'15m'` for codes, `'1h'` for links | |
| `emailChange.digits` | `8` | 6 to 9. |
| `emailChange.maxAttempts` | `5` | Wrong guesses per code, counted before each comparison. |
| `emailChange.revertTtl` | `'7d'` | The minimum; a shorter value is refused at startup. |
| `emailChange.blockAfterRevert` | `'30d'` | |

Your own `beforeEmailChange` hook runs after the fresh-auth check and before anything is issued. It is given the normalised new address; refuse with a code that does not reveal whether that address is taken.

## Limits

- **One change per revert window.** While a revert link is live the account cannot start another change, even when the user made the first one themselves. A typo the user noticed late waits for the link to expire, or for support.
- **The hold covers the library's flows only.** Sign-up, change requests and confirms refuse a held address. Your own user-creating paths must call `isAddressHeld`; the library cannot see them. Sign-up also checks the hold before its insert, so a race can slip through. When the old address gets an account anyway, the revert cannot restore it: the account is locked out (no session, no reset) until the owner finishes or support clears it, however long that takes.
- **Sign-up on a held address is matched in answer and round-trip count, not in timing.** It gives the taken-address answer and mail and makes the same number of store round trips (four), but where a taken address does a failed insert and a lookup, a held one does two reads, and a new address does an insert and a token write. Its timing matches neither exactly; the difference is one round trip's worth of write cost.
- **A revert keeps every second factor, the intruder's too.** If the intruder enrolled a factor while they held the account, the owner's reset after the revert asks for it and the owner cannot pass it. For that case support verifies the owner outside the account (the old mailbox alone proves nothing: the intruder may read it too), then deletes the factor and its recovery codes through the two-factor store (`deleteFactor(userId)` and `replaceRecoveryCodes(userId, [])`) and has the owner reset the password. The `email.change_reverted` row (`review: true`) is where to start.
- **A new address's request limit can be spent by others.** `email-change-address` (3 an hour) counts requests to an address from every account, so anyone signed in who knows it can stall changes to it for an hour.
